extracted.intended_audience: general readers and aviation/transportation safety stakeholders (journalists, regulators, engineers, enthusiasts)
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article documenting a specific aviation safety incident (the 2013 Boeing 787 Dreamliner battery problems), summarizing timeline, investigative findings, regulatory actions, and technical issues related to lithium-ion battery safety. Useful for readers seeking a consolidated account of causes, responses, and recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounding until modifications reduce battery overheating/fire risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAA issued an emergency airworthiness directive ordering all U.S.-based airlines to ground their Boeing 787s until yet-to-be-determined modifications were made to the electrical system to reduce the risk of the battery overheating or catching fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounding is justified when the risk of battery overheating or catching fire cannot be acceptably mitigated in service; return-to-service requires implementation of modifications that demonstrably reduce that risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design requirements to mitigate effects of internal short circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: The NTSB determined the probable cause was an internal short circuit within a cell which led to a thermal runaway that cascaded to adjacent cells, and found that the incident resulted from Boeing's failure to incorporate design requirements to mitigate the most severe effects of an internal short circuit within an APU battery cell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Battery and system design must include requirements and measures specifically aimed at preventing, containing, or mitigating the worst-case effects of an internal cell short circuit (prevent cascade, venting, fire spread).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and testing of worst-case battery failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Boeing's engineers 'failed to consider and test for worst-case battery failures' according to the NTSB summary of findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification and design verification should include analysis and testing of worst‑case failure modes (e.g., thermal runaway, internal shorts, dendrite formation) to ensure systems remain safe under extreme conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Battery manufacturing quality control to prevent inspection-evading defects
rubrics_metrics.description: The NTSB assigned blame to GS Yuasa of Japan for battery manufacturing methods that could introduce defects not caught by inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers must employ processes and quality control that prevent introduction of latent defects; inspections and acceptance tests should be capable of detecting manufacturing flaws that could lead to thermal runaway or short-circuiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of battery chemistry with lower thermal runaway energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The article notes that lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO2) electrodes are known for their thermal runaway hazard and that newer types (such as LiFePO4 and LiMn2O4) provide less reaction energy during thermal runaway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, choose battery chemistries with inherently lower propensity and energy release in thermal runaway (e.g., LiFePO4, LiMn2O4) over higher‑energy chemistries like LiCoO2 for aircraft applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Containment of fires within battery systems (enclosures / containment measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAA allowed return to service after changes were made to better contain fires within their battery systems; Boeing added an enclosure to contain the battery which added weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Battery installations should include robust enclosures/containment that prevent fire, smoke, or vented electrolyte from affecting adjacent systems or the cabin; containment solutions must be validated even if they incur weight/operational penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of active fire-suppression (vs. only smoke detection) in battery compartments
rubrics_metrics.description: The article states there are no fire-suppression systems in the electrical compartments holding batteries, only smoke detectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electrical compartments that house batteries should be evaluated for active fire suppression or other mitigation measures in addition to detection, rather than relying solely on smoke detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory certification oversight and enforcement of special conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The FAA approved a 787 battery in 2007 with nine 'special conditions' and the NTSB criticized the FAA for failing to identify the design deficiency during the type design certification process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators must ensure that special conditions and certification requirements are comprehensive and enforced; oversight should include scrutiny of battery design, manufacturing, testing, and installed configuration to ensure compliance with approved conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability and conformity of installed batteries to approved design/manufacturer
rubrics_metrics.description: A battery approved by the FAA (through Mobile Power Solutions) was made by Rose Electronics using Kokam cells, but the batteries installed in the 787 were made by Yuasa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Installations must conform to the specific, certified design and components; supply-chain and configuration control are required so that installed batteries match those approved in the type certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention and detection of cascade thermal runaway among cells
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal short circuit in a cell led to a thermal runaway that cascaded to adjacent cells, releasing smoke and fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cell and pack design, spacing, thermal barriers, and electrical architecture should prevent a failure in one cell from propagating to neighbors; include vent paths and barriers to reduce cascade risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cell-level monitoring and detection beyond simple voltage limits
rubrics_metrics.description: JTSB said the main battery reached a maximum voltage of 31 V (within the 32 V limit) but had a sudden unexplained voltage drop to near zero and all cells had signs of thermal damage before runaway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring systems should not rely solely on pack-level voltage limits; include cell-level monitoring, anomaly detection for sudden drops, and state indicators that can identify developing thermal or electrical faults before catastrophic failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems integration between battery management and crew alerting systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern remained that solutions might not cover problems arising from poor systems integration between the engine indicating and crew alerting system (EICAS) and the battery management system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Battery management must be integrated effectively with aircraft alerting and indication systems so crews receive timely, accurate warnings and appropriate crew procedures can be initiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multi-agency investigation and timely reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The NTSB, JTSB, FAA and other agencies opened investigations and hearings; reports and recommendations were issued (NTSB report Dec 1, 2014, and others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious incidents should prompt coordinated multi‑agency investigation, public reporting of findings, and issuance of recommendations to manufacturers and regulators to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory coordination for international grounding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the FAA action, multiple national authorities (e.g., Japan, Europe, Chile, India, Qatar, Ethiopia) grounded their fleets, ultimately grounding all 50 aircraft worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National aviation authorities should coordinate responses to systemic safety risks revealed by incidents, including harmonized grounding or operational restrictions where appropriate.
